items.title: fix(eval): correct benchmark execution semantics
items.body:
### Motivation

- The previous benchmark aborted the entire suite on a single malformed stage output and reported misleading schema/compliance and category metrics. 
- The judge contract used by the benchmark deviated from the compact production `JudgeVerdict` + trusted materialization path, enabling silent repairs and invalid evidence acceptance. 
- Important-finding probe matching was conflated with semantic finding-category accuracy, producing incorrect category accuracy numbers. 
- The benchmark must preserve BlindGuard semantics and record per-case typed failures so real Codex-native runs can be trusted and audited.

### Description

- Execute every case independently and record per-case stage outcomes without aborting the suite, introducing `StageStatus` and typed `FailureCategory` to classify forward/verifier/judge/evidence/orchestration/provider failures. 
- Request the compact `JudgeVerdict` contract from the judge and materialize it with `materialize_judge_verdict(...)`, failing closed on invalid evidence rather than normalizing or repairing malformed output. 
- Replace hard-coded schema-compliance metrics with derived rates computed from actual stage attempts and successful decodes, and separate important-finding text-probe detection from true finding-category accuracy by comparing the trusted persisted verdict categories. 
- Add suite metadata (suite hash, git revision, generated timestamp), per-case execution_mode, and persist a deterministic 40-case report artifact (path: `reports/benchmark-v1/deterministic.json`); update `fixtures/evaluation/cases.json`, tests, and docs to reflect the honest execution semantics.

### Testing

- Ran formatting and lint gates: `cargo fmt --all -- --check` and `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings`, which passed. 
- Ran unit and integration tests and deterministic evaluation: `cargo test --workspace` and focused CLI tests (`cargo test -p flect-cli --test evaluation` and `cargo test -p flect-cli --bin flect eval::tests`), which passed; added new eval unit tests covering typed schema failures and closed evidence-validation failures. 
- Executed the deterministic 40-case offline run (`cargo run -p flect-cli -- eval --output reports/benchmark-v1/deterministic.json`), producing the persistent report artifact with 40 attempted / 40 persisted / 0 failed fixture cases (deterministic plumbing only). 
- One environment-specific issue remains: several `flect-runner` HTTP/Responses integration tests that expect proxied/mock network behavior failed in this runtime because provider HTTP interactions were intercepted and returned authentication responses; this indicates the current environment cannot reliably simulate the provider network surface or spawn fresh Codex verifier/judge agents, so no real Codex-native 40-case run was performed and no live-model performance claims are made.

items.title: Add search correctness benchmark
items.body:
Bottom of a six-part stack. This PR adds only the measurement harness. The behaviour changes it was written to guard sit in the PRs above it.

### What Changed

- Added a deterministic 50-query / 66-document synthetic search benchmark under `packages/search-client/src/benchmark`.
- Cases cover exact and malformed citations, ambiguous queries, titles, party names, provider ids, body phrases, no-answer queries, court browse, date filters, and 10 short-word queries.
- Wired it into CI against pinned Meilisearch 1.12.0, with regression gating and a JSON artifact holding top-k ids, engine scores, and failure labels.
- No retrieval or ranking behaviour changes here. `packages/search-client/src/index.ts` is untouched.

### Why

Search had a substring-matching defect: a query for `test` matched `testimony` and `testator`. Fixing relevance without a fixed case set means trading one silent failure for another, so the measurement lands first and the fix lands on top of it.

The baseline recorded here is therefore deliberately the *broken* behaviour, not a target. It is the number the PRs above have to beat.

### Implementation Notes

- Baseline in this PR: overall top-1/top-3 `0.9231`; exact citation/document-id top-1 `1.0`; short-word precision `0.20`; evidence recall `1.0`; no-answer precision `0`; malformed-citation no-result rate `0.3333`; ambiguity surfaced `1.0`; three date-filter search errors.
- Metric floors are minimums and error counts are maximums, so a later PR that improves a metric passes without editing the baseline. Tightening a floor is a deliberate edit.
- The fixture corpus is synthetic. It contains no raw legal text and no client matter data.
- `docs/prds/search.md` describes the old ranker as a four-value bucket; the implementation has six (`0-5`). The PRD was deliberately not edited.
- No migrations, routes, workspaces, required environment variables, `packages/legal-schema` changes, or architecture map changes. No new package dependency. CI adds a pinned local Meilisearch service and a report artifact.

### Testing

- `pnpm typecheck`, `pnpm lint`, `pnpm format:check` all pass on this layer.
- `pnpm vitest run packages/search-client services/api/src/routes/legal-search`: 112 passed, 14 skipped.
- `SEARCH_BENCHMARK_HOST=http://127.0.0.1:7700 SEARCH_BENCHMARK_API_KEY=<local key> pnpm benchmark:search` was run against local Meilisearch 1.12.0 and the full top-k, score, and failure-label report inspected.
- Not tested: no production corpus and no production Meilisearch rollout was exercised. No UI change, so no UI pass.

### Risks / Follow-Ups

Two known weaknesses in this harness are deliberately not fixed here, because both change the reported numbers and so need their own measured PR:

- `ratio()` returns `1` when the denominator is zero, so `shortWordPrecision` scores a perfect 1.0 for a query that returns nothing at all. The top-1 floor currently catches this, but the precision metric alone is satisfiable by returning nothing.
- `engineRankingScoreCoverage` excludes errored cases entirely, so a search failure silently improves coverage. Relatedly, `maximumSearchErrors` counts errors without identifying which cases produced them, so a new failure is invisible if an existing one starts passing.

`storedSearchP95Ms` measures Meilisearch's own `processingTimeMs`, which is engine time only. It does not cover application-side ranking or snippet work, so it cannot detect a regression there.

The three `date_filtered_query` cases record `search_error` because `toMeiliFilters` emits string range comparisons on `dateDecided`, which Meilisearch rejects. That is a live defect on `/api/search`, not a fixture problem, and it is tracked for its own PR rather than fixed here.

### Rollout / Operations

CI-only in this PR. Nothing ships to production from this layer. CI uploads the benchmark report so failed cases stay inspectable.

items.body:
## Summary

Implements the "publish benchmark datasets" idea (#8) and closes out "improve docs for new users" (#9).

## #8 — Version-controlled scientific benchmarks

A single suite that pins the values the model must reproduce **on every commit** — regression tests for **scientific** correctness, not just software correctness. If a change moves any of them, CI fails and the diff names the drifted quantity *and the published source it drifted from*.

Every benchmark comes from **bundled data or a pure function** — no external file, no `mufflyaccess` — so it runs in CI as a **hard gate with no skips**:

| Benchmark | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Physician retirement survival | S(60)=0.80, S(65)=0.55, S(70)=0.30, S(75)=0.12, S(80)=0.03 | HWSM Exhibit 17 / FutureDocs |
| Capacity-survey adequacy | 0.948 (5.2% gap) | Zarek 2025 PTJ |
| Published base-year shortfalls | Dall 2021 940/10.6%, Zarek 12,070/5.2%, Dall 2013 1,814/11.0% | the source studies |
| Validated 2023 workforce total | 1,306 (national ABOG+ABU); 1,027 ABOG-only; 1,303 CONUS | mufflyaccess contract v3.0.0 |
| FutureDocs participation | female FTE peaks 0.675 @50, collapses by 80; rows sum to 1 | FutureDocs Fig 9 |

- **`tests/testthat/test-scientific-benchmarks.R`** — the guard (21 assertions). Loose "read-off-a-chart" anchors use absolute-difference checks (testthat's `tolerance` is relative and too strict for e.g. 0.117 vs a charted 0.12); exact curves are pinned tight as regression locks.
- **`docs/BENCHMARKS.md`** — the source table, why each is load-bearing, how to run, and how to add a new one (named source + canonical accessor + prefer no external data).

## #9 — New-user orientation

This turned out to be **already covered** by the README's `## Orientation (start here)` section (added in the recent file-layout refactor), which answers all four questions from the request — *what question does this answer / what inputs / vs Markov / vs deterministic* — plus "what's validated." Rather than add a competing `ORIENTATION.md` that would drift from it, I linked the new `BENCHMARKS.md` into that section's "Deeper reading" line.

items.title: fix(backtest): keep excess_return consistent with corrected benchmark_return
items.body:
## Summary

- BaseEngine.run_backtest() corrects the displayed benchmark_return once an external benchmark's price series contains a non-positive-prior-price bar, but never recomputes excess_return from that same corrected value
- Recomputes excess_return right where benchmark_return is already corrected, so the two fields remain consistent for this corrected benchmark path

## Why

Issue #872 replaced the fragile pct_change-based return calculation with a safe price relative (buy_and_hold_return) for the displayed benchmark_return, after finding it could report numbers like +39,560% where the true return was -42.7%. calc_metrics() has its own internal re-derivation of the same total, still using the exact (1 + bench_ret).prod() - 1 pattern #872 found unsafe. base.py corrects the displayed field but never re-derives excess_return from the corrected value, so the metrics dict can become self-contradictory: benchmark_return reads correctly while excess_return implies a different number, both in the same JSON output the backtest tool returns to the LLM.

I audited every benchmark-derived metric in calc_metrics() (benchmark_return, excess_return, information_ratio, tracking_error, benchmark_beta). Only excess_return is affected. The other three are computed from the per-bar bench_ret series directly, which is already the corrected, #872-safe series by the time it reaches calc_metrics().

## Changes

- agent/backtest/engines/base.py: after the existing benchmark_metadata override, excess_return is recomputed as total_return minus the corrected benchmark_return, but only when an external benchmark was actually resolved. The internal-basket-benchmark path (no config["benchmark"]) is untouched.
- agent/tests/test_benchmark_excess_return_consistency.py: two new regression tests. One runs the real production path (ChinaAEngine.run_backtest, real calc_metrics(), only the network-dependent resolve_benchmark() fetch is stubbed) with a benchmark price series crossing a non-positive-prior-price bar, and asserts total_return minus excess_return equals benchmark_return. The other is a control confirming the fix does not touch excess_return when no external benchmark is configured.

items.title: fix(test): make the corrector benchmark gate load-invariant
items.body:
## What

`ContactsImportCorrectorBenchmark` asserted an **absolute wall-clock bound** (`maxPerCallMs < 1500`) on a machine running ~4,300 tests in parallel. It went red on **unmodified main** at 2,836 ms while the machine was also running Codex reviews and Xcode builds, then passed on every rerun.

## I measured before changing anything

"Flaky gate" and "real latency problem" look identical from one red run, and 2,836 ms against a live 3,000 ms `WordCorrectionStep` cap would have been a product problem, not a test problem.

| condition | 2000 terms | ratio 2000/500 |
|---|---|---|
| idle, 10 samples | 373 – 544 ms (median 390) | 2.85 – 3.93 |
| 14-core busy-loop load | 446 ms | 3.65 |
| inside a full 4,346-test suite run | 382 ms | 3.87 |

**The failure is not reproducible in any condition I could construct.** Every measurement sits 3–4x under the old bar. The reported 2,836 ms needed a pathological machine state.

## Fix

Assert the **growth ratio**, which contention cannot inflate — load scales both buckets together, so it divides out. That is verified, not assumed: the ratio under 14-core load (3.65) lands inside the idle range, as does the full-suite run (3.87).

Across 14 samples in all three conditions the ratio spans **2.85 – 4.41**. 4x the terms costs ~4x the time, so this is linear. The bar of 8 sits at ~1.8x the worst observed and at half the 16x an O(n²) regression would produce.

A ratio alone would miss a uniform constant-factor blowup, so one absolute bound remains as a **secondary net at 10 s**, where load cannot reach it (worst ever observed anywhere is 3,132 ms).

That bound is deliberately **not** the 3,000 ms product cap. Whether a real user with a very large address book can approach that cap is a product question — filed separately as #1865 with the measured distribution. A load-sensitive test on a shared machine cannot police it, and pretending it could is what made this gate flaky.

## Controls

- **Two-way:** dropping the bar to 3.0 turns the test red on the real measurement (3.55x observed), so the assertion is live and reads real data rather than passing vacuously.
- Full suite: **4,344 tests in 414 suites passed**, plus 179 in 18 suites.
- `scripts/build-dev-app.sh` succeeded.

## One correction worth recording

An early single cold-start sample showed 6.05x growth and I read it as superlinear. Ten paired samples disproved that — the cold run was the outlier, not the signal. #1865 is filed with the corrected linear figure.

Test-only. No `Sources/` change.

**Lane:** Code

Closes #1805

items.title: release: v0.126.0 — sort / sort_by builtins (#580), corrected benchmarks, new bench suites
items.body:
Closes #580.

machin had **no sort** — not a builtin, not in any of the 16 framework modules — so
every program needing ordered output hand-rolled one.

## Why this mattered

It cost machin the authoring-cost comparison it is positioned on. Same task in both
languages (read a file, count word frequencies, print top 5 by count then
alphabetically), tiktoken `o200k_base`:

| | tokens | lines | vs Rust |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| machin (before) | 218 | 26 | **+21%** |
| rust | 180 | 19 | — |
| **machin (after)** | **151** | **17** | **−16%** |

The entire difference was the sort. Rust does it in one `sort_by` line; machin
needed a 12-line selection sort — 90 of its 218 tokens.

Beyond tokens: what an agent hand-writes under time pressure is the O(n²) version,
and comparator tie-breaks are easy to get subtly wrong. Both are avoidable.

## API

```
sort(xs)            // ascending, for []int / []float / []string
sort_by(xs, less)   // ordered by less(a, b) bool; the comparator may capture
```

```
sort_by(keys(counts), func(a, b) {
    if counts[a] != counts[b] { return counts[a] > counts[b] }
    return a < b
})
```

## Two design decisions worth reviewing

**It returns a NEW slice rather than sorting in place.** MFL slices share backing
storage — `b := a` aliases, and so does passing one to a function (both verified).
An in-place sort would silently reorder every alias, which is the same hazard that
made in-place `realloc` unsound in #578. Copy-then-sort also matches slice-range,
which already always returns a fresh copy. There's a test asserting the input and
its aliases come out untouched.

**It is STABLE**, via a bottom-up merge sort rather than `qsort` — `qsort` is not
stable, and its comparator cannot portably carry an MFL closure environment. The
comparator is asked *"must b precede a?"* (i.e. `less(b, a)`), which needs one call
per comparison instead of two **and** yields stability for free: when neither
element is less than the other the predicate is false, so the earlier element goes
first. That means sorting by one key then another composes the way you'd expect.

`sort()` on an element type with no natural ordering is refused at compile time
with a message that names the fix:

```
error: sort: element type mfl_P has no ordering — use sort_by(xs, less) and say how to compare them
```

## Tests

Seven cases: ordered element types incl. negatives/empty/single, non-mutation of
input **and aliases**, comparator ordering, stability across two equal-key groups,
a capturing closure as comparator, the compile-time rejection, and a 500-element
sort verified fully ordered (exercises the merge's width doubling past pass one).

Documented in `machin guide` in the same change, per AGENTS.md.

Full suite green — `ok machin 178.854s`.

  * Added `sort_by` for stable sorting with custom comparator functions.
  * Sorting returns a new slice without modifying the original.

items.title: fix(chat): correct benchmark ChatBox message order; add collapsed benchmark header digest
items.body:
Two fixes to the benchmark experience, reported together.

## 1. ChatBox messages appeared out of order during benchmark runs

The benchmark runner calls `ChatManager.sendToLLM()` directly instead of going through `startConversation()`, so `conversationState.currentRequestId` stays `null` for an entire run. `findActivityPanelElement()` keyed its lookup off:

```js
document.getElementById(`thinkingProcess_${currentRequestId || Date.now()}`) || document.querySelector('.thinking-process')
```

A fresh `Date.now()` can never match an element id, so every resolution fell through to `querySelector('.thinking-process')` — which returns the **first** panel in the transcript. Meanwhile `addThinkingMessage()` kept appending new panels at the bottom. The result: the LLM's context, tool inventory, and per-round execution output were all filed into the oldest panel at the top of the chat while the benchmark's headline panels stacked below it.

The same `Date.now()` id had a second failure mode: two panels opened within one millisecond shared an id, and opening the second removed the first along with its steps.

**Fix:** track the panel that was last opened and resolve against it, falling back to the *newest* panel on screen rather than the oldest. Detached panels get a sequential id instead of a timestamp. Clearing the transcript drops the tracked panel and round group, since the benchmark clears between tests.

## 2. Collapsed benchmark interface now shows a run digest

Collapsing the interface hides the progress panel — exactly when a long run gets left unattended. The header line now carries: run state, tests completed / total, pass/fail tally, elapsed time, and the test in flight.

`RUNNING · 8/24 (33%) · ✅ 6 · ❌ 2 · ⏱ 03:41 · ▶ current_test`

The digest keeps its own tally rather than reading the progress panel's DOM counters, which are never reset in the main window and so accumulate across runs. Its timer ticks off the existing one-second interval, so elapsed time keeps moving while collapsed. Collapsed height grows 60px → 68px for the second line; the subtitle gives up its slot.

## Testing

- 1438/1438 unit tests pass.
- 4 new cases in `chat-activity-panel.test.js` covering the detached-request path. Verified they fail against the old code and pass against the new — including a frozen-clock case for the same-millisecond id collision.
- New `benchmark-header-status.test.js`, 9 cases: each run state, the real progress-callback path, HTML/attribute escaping of test ids, and a missing framework.
- Collapsed layout measured and screenshotted in a real browser render (container 68px, digest bottom edge at 60px).

## Known issues left out of scope

Both were flagged rather than silently absorbed:

1. Benchmark runs never call `endConversation()`, so their activity panels keep spinning instead of collapsing into a completion summary.
2. `resetProgressCounters()` is only wired into the fallback-window path, so the progress panel's own completed/passed/failed counters accumulate across reruns in the main window. The header digest sidesteps this with its own tally; the panel itself still shows inflated numbers on a second run.

items.title: Correct performance benchmark fixture and diagnostics
items.body:
## Summary

- make the simulation benchmark emit structured JSON with configurable seed, world mode, step count, timing, contact, solver, live-agent, and physical-body diagnostics
- add a one-stream-period `agents_only` ablation that suppresses terrain generation without changing production physics
- replace the collision-prone two-unit benchmark placement with a deterministic four-unit lattice
- add geometry and streamed-world invariants covering the 37-agent boundary

## Root cause

The legacy benchmark placed agents on a two-unit grid. Agent index 36—the 37th agent—was placed at `(8, 8)`. Streamed terrain for that chunk is generated within 0.5 units of nominal `(8, 8)`, and both colliders have radius 0.5. The benchmark therefore introduced a guaranteed initial overlap at 37 agents.

Solved collision impulses caused structural damage and fragmentation, multiplying physical bodies and contacts. This made the reported 37–40-agent discontinuity look like a raw scaling threshold when it was primarily a fixture collision.

## Predeclared evidence

items.title: Benchmark STT candidates over a corrected benchmark set
items.body:
Closes #39.

## What

Adds a **batch STT benchmark** that runs the configured STT candidates across every corrected segment in a chosen benchmark split (`test_frozen` / `validation`), instead of one selected segment at a time. This is the core benchmark needed before choosing a base STT model.

## How

- **`localEvents.ts` — `getSttBenchmarkSetSegments(events, split)`** (pure): selects the segments whose *latest* membership resolves to `split` (latest-event-wins, matching `reconstructRecentSegments`), keeps only those with a resolvable `audio_ref`, and returns them in a deterministic order (`sessionId` then `segmentId`).
- **`index.ts` — `benchmark:run-set-stt`**: reads the event log **once** so every segment scores against the same correction snapshot and appended results can't shift later lookups; iterates the split **sequentially**; reuses the existing single-segment runner (now accepts a shared events snapshot); appends the **same `stt_benchmark_result` events** (candidate + CER score metadata — no new event type); streams `queued/running/done/failed` progress; and **isolates per-segment failures** (one bad segment never aborts the run).
- **preload/renderer**: a `Benchmark set` panel with a split selector, live progress counts, current-segment line, and a per-segment outcome/failure list. Single-segment `Benchmark latest` / per-history `Benchmark` still work and are mutually disabled with the batch run to avoid concurrent STT.
- **docs**: added a smoke-test step for the batch flow.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] Run STT benchmark candidates over a corrected benchmark split.
- [x] Every result stays tied to `session_id`, `segment_id`, `audio_ref`, and candidate metadata (same event schema as before).
- [x] Existing single-segment benchmark still works.
- [x] UI reports progress and per-segment failures clearly.

Out of scope (untouched): fine-tuning, charts/dashboard, automatic model selection, LLM/math-transform stages, cloud execution.

## Verification

- `npm run typecheck` — clean.
- `npm run build` — clean (main/preload/renderer all build).
- Unit-checked the correctness-critical selector `getSttBenchmarkSetSegments` with 10 synthetic-event cases (split filtering, latest-membership-wins reassignment in both directions, `audio_ref` resolution incl. out-of-order events, exclusion when no audio / no membership, deterministic ordering, `hasCorrection`, malformed-event tolerance) — all pass.

Refs #44

## Summary

This PR builds the reproducible evidence pipeline for the standalone CSC3 symmetric assembly demo:

- adds an independent sparse serial symbolic/numeric reference;
- validates generated Tet4/Hex8 cases and Abaqus C3D4/C3D8 inputs;
- records phase-separated symbolic, numeric, and amortized timings;
- adds WindHub-aware benchmark orchestration with strict Git LFS and formal-host preflight checks;
- recomputes CSV statistics, speedups, correctness thresholds, and performance gates instead of trusting summaries;
- generates a deterministic 13-section Chinese test report from hash-bound evidence;
- checks in a clearly labelled macOS ARM64 `LOCAL_SMOKE` evidence bundle and report.

The candidate delivery path remains deterministic parallel symbolic assembly plus OpenMP atomic numeric assembly. Serial code is used only as the independent correctness/performance reference.

## Correctness contract

The evidence enforces:

$$
e_F =
\frac{\lVert K_p-K_s\rVert_F}
{\max(\lVert K_s\rVert_F,10^{-30})}
\le 10^{-8},
$$

$$
e_{\max}
\le
10^{-10}+10^{-8}\max |K_s|,
$$

$$
e_u =
\frac{\lVert u_p-u_s\rVert_2}
{\max(\lVert u_s\rVert_2,10^{-30})}
\le 10^{-8},
\qquad
r_{\mathrm{rel}}\le 10^{-10}.
$$

The JSON evidence carries the independent reference scale used to recompute the absolute-error tolerance for the benchmark root and the fixed Tet4/Hex8 validation cases. The performance CSV remains exactly 30 columns.

Formal delivery evidence now requires one same-run sequence of configure, build, CTest, and benchmark tasks. The verifier binds task order, commands, cwd, OpenMP environment, arguments, output paths, source identity, and canonical WindHub LFS identity.

Source and input are revalidated after build, before benchmark, and after benchmark. Smoke evidence cannot be promoted to formal `PASS`.

items.title: feat(bench): correctness benchmark (precision/recall) para CSP + cookies
items.body:
## O que

Um **benchmark de correção** para os detectores determinísticos do Fracta: precisão / recall / F1 medidos sobre um corpus rotulado por **ground-truth externo** (CSP spec / OWASP / MDN) — não pelo que o nosso próprio detector faz.

Fecha o gap "10/10": até agora a acurácia era *afirmada*; agora é **medida, reproduzível e guardada no CI**.

## Resultado (24 casos)

| Categoria | Casos | Precisão | Recall | F1 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| CSP | 16 | 100.0% | 73.9% | 0.850 |
| Cookies | 8 | 100.0% | 100.0% | 1.000 |
| **Geral** | 24 | **100.0%** | **80.0%** | 0.889 |

- **Precisão 100%** — zero falso-positivo nas regras que cobrimos.
- **Recall 80%** — e os *únicos* misses são os **2 gaps documentados** (`csp-no-frame-ancestors`, `csp-no-form-action`). Um número honesto mostra os limites em vez de escondê-los.

## Honestidade por design

O corpus inclui **de propósito** casos-gap: políticas com problemas que um scanner completo emitiria mas o Fracta ainda **não** cobre → viram false-negative honesto. Sem isso, o recall seria 100% por construção (mentira).

## Guarda de regressão

`bench.test.ts` roda no CI e quebra se:
- a precisão regredir (`< 99%` → começamos a falso-positivar),
- o recall cair (`< 80%`),
- **ou** aparecer qualquer FN que **não** seja uma regra-gap declarada (regressão silenciosa de cobertura).

## Arquivos
- `packages/web-scan/src/bench/metrics.ts` — precisão/recall/F1 puro (+ 5 testes)

items.body:
…fe tracemalloc, skip dead tempo analysis (#116, #117, #118, #119)

#116: run_parse/run_map/run_frames and the detect-patterns writer all used json.dumps(..., indent=2) for machine-only intermediates that are never hand-read, inflating write/read cost 2-3x for no benefit. Switched all four to compact separators=(',', ':'); human-facing report writers (benchmark results) are untouched.

#117: the benchmark harness measured the wrong production code paths - tracker.parser (the slow full parser) instead of tracker.parser_fast, and EnhancedPatternDetector (the serial fallback) instead of ParallelPatternDetector (the actual default). Every benchmark_*_stage method also ran its work inside `with profiler.profile(name):` (whose body already stops tracemalloc) and then called `_end_profiling` a second time after the `with` block exited, hitting an already-stopped trace and silently falling back to reporting current RSS instead of the measured peak. profile() now yields a ProfileHandle populated exactly once; the redundant second call is gone. find_test_files also now sorts its glob so a directory scan produces the same file order across runs. (Not attempted this pass: a committed regression-gate baseline with a percent-threshold comparison, and a committed deterministic fixture set to replace the directory glob - both are net-new tooling/design decisions, not bug fixes, and are left for a follow-up.)

#118: every profiler (utils.profiling's profile_memory_usage decorator and PerformanceContext, plus benchmarks.performance_suite's PerformanceProfiler) called the process-global tracemalloc.start()/stop() independently. Nesting one inside another - e.g. a @profile_memory_usage-decorated function called inside a PerformanceContext - let the inner stop() tear down tracing for the still-running outer profiler, whose later get_traced_memory() then raised and was silently swallowed into an RSS fallback. All three now go through a shared reference-counted _tracemalloc_acquire/_tracemalloc_release in utils.profiling, so only the outermost profiler actually starts/stops tracing. Also documented (rather than added blocking latency to) the advisory nature of interval-less cpu_percent() readings.

#119: EnhancedPatternDetector's per-pattern tempo analysis (_analyze_pattern_tempo/_analyze_variation_tempos) queries the tempo map using pattern positions as if they were MIDI ticks. In both of main.py's production call sites the tempo map passed in is a fresh default with no real tempo-change data, and the analysis result (registered onto the tempo map object) is never read back - it's pure wasted computation. Added an analyze_tempo=True constructor flag (default preserves existing behavior for any other caller) and pass analyze_tempo=False from both call sites. (Not attempted this pass: threading the parse-stage tempo map through the JSON contract so downstream stages could deserialize instead of reconstruct, and eliminating the events/frames/events reshape - both are real architectural changes serving genuinely different consumer shapes, not a same-session-safe fix, and are left for a follow-up.)

items.title: fix(adapters): GPU adapter correctness fixes, benchmark, and download allocation
items.body:
## Summary

GPU adapter follow-ups: three correctness fixes, one memory-safety fix, a benchmark, and one measured optimization. Core is untouched.

The benchmark came first on purpose, and it paid for itself immediately — it surfaced the use-after-free below.

| commit | what |
|---|---|
| `12c1bdc` | **Vulkan: fail at Open on device-only memory.** The header claimed both upload *and* download paths were implemented; download only ever implemented the host-visible mapped path. On a discrete GPU a graph started cleanly and then threw mid-stream. Now the comment says the truth and `VkDownload` rejects unsupported devices in `Open`, so `graph.start()` fails immediately. Pure GPU segments (upload + compute, result stays on device) are unaffected. |
| `8b91bc5` | **Use the ABI dtype table.** Both adapters hand-rolled a `DtypeSize` switch that omitted `LMFLOW_DTYPE_I64` and `LMFLOW_DTYPE_F16`, so an F16 tensor threw instead of uploading — while the C ABI already exports `lmflow_dtype_size()` covering all nine dtypes. |
| `0ce3870` | 🔴 **Vulkan: retire device memory after all in-flight work.** See below. |
| `5432da8` | **Staged GPU benchmark** (upload / dispatch_enqueue / download / roundtrip at 1/4/24 MB), same JSON shape as `native_throughput.cc` so `compare_reports.py` diffs two runs directly. |
| `be296ed` | **Allocate download buffers uninitialized.** Download allocated with the zero-filling `lmflow_packet_new_buffer` and then overwrote every byte from the device — a wasted full-buffer memset per frame. |
| `c7e5ee8` | **Reject strided buffers in upload.** `LMFlowBuffer` strides are in bytes and non-contiguous layouts are explicitly legal, and `adopt_buffer` accepts arbitrary strides — but `Upload` bulk-copied and ignored strides, so a padded `cv::Mat` row or a sliced numpy view was uploaded as garbage, silently. |

## 🔴 The use-after-free

`Image::Reset` registered its buffer/memory for deferred reclaim under the image's own `ready_`. On the unified-memory path `Upload` only does a host memcpy and never submits, so `ready_` stays `0` — and `ReclaimUpTo` treats `0` as already completed (`0 > completed` is false), freeing the buffer immediately.

A dispatch reading that buffer can still be in flight: `EnqueueUnary` submits without waiting when the input has no timeline value, and the engine destroys the input packet as soon as `Process` returns. The GPU then reads freed device memory.

Fix: retire at the highest issued timeline value. Submits and `Reset` are both serialized by `submit_mutex`, so no submit referencing the image can be in progress, and every submit that could reference it has a value `<=` that bound.

This is the **unified-memory path — i.e. the ARM/mobile main path**. The existing test misses it because its buffers are small enough that the dispatch finishes before the free lands.

## Measured (B1)

llvmpipe, 5 interleaved runs per variant, medians:

```
vk/download/1mb     0.033 -> 0.021 ms  (-37%)
vk/download/4mb     0.229 -> 0.109 ms  (-53%)
vk/download/24mb    2.996 -> 2.037 ms  (-32%, ~0.96 ms/frame)
vk/roundtrip/24mb  20.932 -> 19.942 ms (-4.7%)
vk/upload/*        unchanged (<2%, control)
```

The `upload/*` controls moving <2% is what makes the download numbers trustworthy. The `dispatch_enqueue` rows swing ±50% run to run and attribute nothing.

## Validation

- `ctest` 5/5 with `-DLMFLOW_BUILD_VULKAN_ADAPTER=ON`
- `-DLMFLOW_BUILD_OPENCL_ADAPTER=ON`: builds, and `lmflow_opencl_test` passes on an RTX 5080 (real discrete GPU, `host_unified=no`)
- Use-after-free: reproduced as a SIGSEGV on the driver's worker thread with a tight upload→dispatch loop; clean after the fix at 1/4/24 MB

- strides: a 4×8 f32 buffer with 16 bytes of row padding is rejected; the packed equivalent still uploads

**Caveat worth knowing:** the local Vulkan ICD only exposes llvmpipe (the NVIDIA Vulkan driver is version-mismatched), so nothing here is verified on Vulkan against real discrete hardware — including, by construction, A1's device-only branch. OpenCL *is* verified on the RTX 5080.

## Deliberately not done

- **Vulkan staging read-back** for device-only memory — real code that cannot be verified locally; failing loudly at `Open` is the honest interim state.
- **Device memory / command-resource pooling** (per-frame `vkAllocateMemory`, command buffer and descriptor set alloc+free). This is the largest remaining win but needs a working Vulkan device to validate; the same applies to OpenCL's per-frame `clCreateBuffer`.
- **Per-frame shader cache key** (the whole SPIR-V blob is memcpy'd into a `std::string` key and hashed on every dispatch; OpenCL hashes the full source). Real but ~1 µs against a ~20 µs enqueue, and below this harness's noise floor — not worth landing unmeasured.
- **No OpenCL benchmark yet.** Now that the RTX 5080 turns out to be usable through OpenCL, that is the obvious next step and would let the pooling work be measured on real hardware.

## Why this skill and not a routing skill

Routing (which tool for which question) is already handled by tool descriptions and `SERVER_INSTRUCTIONS`. A second copy would be redundant.

What nothing covers today is the multi-grant case, where the decisions interact: exercising ISOs raises AMT exposure in the same year selling RSUs raises ordinary income, and both compete for the same cash. That is a workflow, not a calculation, which is exactly what a skill is for.

The skill:
- **Intake protocol.** Ask for everything missing in one consolidated question, not field by field across turns. Ask for the ticker first, since it resolves growth and volatility.
- **Sequencing.** Run `qsbs_check` early when it might apply, because a five-year holding period reorders everything else.
- **Ordering.** Deadlines before dollar impact. An expiring option is lost permanently; a tax optimization merely gets less good.
- **Honesty about the gap.** Requires naming the specific interactions a sum of independent calculations misses, which is also the honest case for the beta.

The skill instructs the model to reproduce `next_steps` URLs verbatim, including query params. items.body:
## Summary

Phase 8b - the head-to-head comparison benchmark that turns Snipz's correctness claim into a single chart. Same workload, same cap, three backends side-by-side.

**The headline result, on real Postgres:**

| Backend | Successes | Final spend | Cap held? | Duration |
|---|---:|---:|:---:|---:|
| **Snipz** (Postgres) | 50 / 1000 | **\$5.00** | yes | 3.6s |
| LiteLLM `BudgetManager` | 1000 / 1000 | \$100.00 (20x cap) | no | 0.03s |
| Shekel | 1000 / 1000 | \$100.00 (20x cap) | no | 0.03s |

Snipz is ~120x slower because it does the actual work (transaction + row lock + ledger insert). The competitors are fast because they skip the lock. At 1000 concurrent on a \$5 cap, every competitor attempt commits.

## What's in this PR

- **`benchmarks/adapters/`** - `BenchmarkAdapter` Protocol + three implementations (Snipz on testcontainers Postgres; LiteLLM on its in-memory dict; Shekel via its internal `_record_spend`)
- **`benchmarks/competitor_comparison.py`** - the harness. Registry-based; supports `--only snipz,litellm` for partial runs
- **`tests/test_competitor_benchmark.py`** - protocol conformance + anti-claim assertions (if LiteLLM/Shekel ever stop overshooting, our adapter has drifted from the libraries' actual API)
- **`bench-competitors` extra** in pyproject.toml - opt-in install: `pip install snipz[bench-competitors]`
- **Sdist bug fix**: `tests/test_benchmark.py` and `tests/test_competitor_benchmark.py` import from `benchmarks/` but `benchmarks/` was already excluded. Both test files are now excluded from sdist too - rebuilding from source no longer hits ImportError.
- **Version bump 0.1.0 -> 0.2.0** + matching `__version__` + README status line update to v0.2.x.

## Honest race window

The competitor adapters use a 1 ms `asyncio.sleep` between cap-check and cost-record, simulating where the LLM call sits in real workflows. Without it the GIL serializes the read-modify-write fast enough to hide the race. Real LLM calls are 100-2000 ms - the simulated window is **100-2000x shorter than production**, which is conservative.

## Test plan

- [x] 148 tests pass on SQLite default (including 8 new benchmark tests)
- [x] ruff clean on src/ tests/ benchmarks/
- [x] mypy strict clean across 29 source files
- [x] Wheel installs in a fresh Python 3.13 venv and reports `snipz.__version__ == "0.2.0"`

- [ ] After merge: tag `v0.2.0`, push, the new CI workflow takes over (verify version, run tests, build, publish to PyPI via OIDC, create GitHub Release)

This is the **first release that goes through the new tag-triggered CI workflow** wired up in PR #2. After this PR merges and the tag is pushed, GitHub Actions handles the rest end-to-end - no manual \`uv publish\`.

items.body:
## The problem

Five files cited **2.635** as the published benchmark result. That figure appears nowhere in the source they link to.

| | value |
|---|---|
| published result | **2.63598+** |
| AlphaEvolve | **2.6358** |
| our evolved solver (`solve_optimized.py`) | **2.635982** |

The README additionally rounded our 2.635982 to **2.6360**, which made a **0.000002** difference read as a win.

## The correction

Against the real published figure our result is a **match**, not a beat. Against AlphaEvolve's 2.6358 there is a real, if small, margin. All seven sites now say so.

The claim is still worth making — a trivial **0.9798** seed evolving to a specialised optimiser's level is the interesting part, and it does not need a "beat" framing to stand up. It now survives someone checking the arithmetic.

## Scope

Documentation and comments only. No code, no config semantics, no tests affected.

`README.md` (2), `examples/circle_packing/README.md` (1), `examples/circle_packing/helix.toml` (2), `examples/circle_packing/solve_optimized.py` (2).

items.title: Fix benchmark correctness and coverage
items.body:
## What changed

- validate concurrency, rounds, duration, timeout, warmup, token limits, and output paths before running
- treat empty or truncated streaming responses and empty non-stream responses as failures
- stop SSE reads immediately at `[DONE]` and preserve HTTP status/usage on mid-stream failures
- size the connection pool to the highest requested concurrency and remove client-side pacing from steady mode
- use provider-compatible token parameters (`max_completion_tokens` for OpenAI, `max_tokens` elsewhere)
- restore Anthropic through its official OpenAI SDK compatibility endpoint
- update the StepFun preset to the verified `step-3.7-flash` model
- remove API-key-prefix logging from the deprecated v0.1 script
- add behavioral tests and enforce them in CI
- correct README and changelog claims

## Why

Several edge cases could produce false-success benchmark results: HTTP 200
responses with no completion, truncated streams, and SSE connections that
remained open after `[DONE]`. The fixed 256-connection pool also made higher
requested concurrency misleading, while invalid zero/negative arguments could
create empty or broken runs. Provider presets had also drifted from current
compatibility behavior.

## Impact

Benchmark reports now distinguish completed responses from empty/truncated
responses, requested concurrency is reflected by the client connection pool,
steady mode measures unpaced endpoint throughput, and current
OpenAI/Anthropic/StepFun presets work with their expected request fields and
model IDs.

## Validation

- `python3 -m py_compile tests4llms-v0.2.py legacy/tests4llms-v0.1.py tests/test_tests4llms.py`
